exams.title: FL1: Chem/Phys
exams.description: Full-length Chem/Phys section: 10 passages and 59 questions in 95 minutes.

items.title: Kinetics of a Bacterial Hydrolase
items.body: Researchers characterized enzyme X, a bacterial hydrolase that converts substrate S to product. Initial reaction velocities (v0) were measured at 25 °C and a fixed enzyme concentration across a range of substrate concentrations (Table 1). The data fit the Michaelis–Menten equation, v0 = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]). In a second experiment, compound I was added at a fixed concentration. Fitting the new data gave an apparent Km of 6.0 mM, while Vmax was unchanged.

questions.stem: What is the Km of enzyme X in the absence of compound I?
questions.explanation: Km is the [S] at which v0 = ½Vmax = 25 µM/s, which Table 1 shows at 2.0 mM. 25 is the velocity, not the Km; 1.0 and 5.0 mM give 16.7 and 35.7 µM/s.

questions.stem: Compound I most likely acts as which type of inhibitor?
questions.explanation: Apparent Km increases while Vmax is unchanged, the signature of competitive inhibition: excess substrate outcompetes the inhibitor. Uncompetitive lowers both; noncompetitive lowers Vmax only; irreversible inhibition lowers effective Vmax.

questions.stem: In the presence of compound I, what is v0 when [S] = 2.0 mM?
questions.explanation: v0 = (50)(2.0)/(6.0 + 2.0) = 12.5 µM/s. 25.0 µM/s is the uninhibited value; 10.0 and 37.5 come from using the wrong Km in the denominator or numerator.

questions.stem: On a Lineweaver–Burk plot of the uninhibited data, the y-intercept equals:
questions.explanation: Lineweaver–Burk: 1/v0 = (Km/Vmax)(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax. The y-intercept is 1/Vmax, the slope is Km/Vmax, and the x-intercept is −1/Km.

questions.stem: If the experiment were repeated with twice the enzyme concentration, how would Vmax and Km change?
questions.explanation: Vmax = kcat[E]total, so doubling enzyme doubles Vmax. Km is an intrinsic property of the enzyme–substrate pair and does not depend on enzyme concentration.

items.title: Optics of a Fluorescence Microscope
items.body: A fluorescence microscope uses a converging objective lens with a focal length of 4.0 mm. A fixed cell sample is placed 5.0 mm in front of the objective. The sample is stained with a dye that absorbs light at 488 nm and emits fluorescence at 520 nm. Light travels from the glass coverslip (n = 1.50) into the surrounding air (n = 1.00) before reaching the objective.

questions.stem: How far from the objective does the image form?
questions.explanation: 1/f = 1/do + 1/di → 1/di = 1/4.0 − 1/5.0 = 1/20, so di = 20 mm. 2.2 mm comes from adding the reciprocals; 9.0 mm adds the distances.

questions.stem: The image formed by the objective is:
questions.explanation: di is positive (real), and m = −di/do = −20/5.0 = −4, so the image is inverted and magnified 4×. Virtual images form only when the object is inside the focal length.

questions.stem: Compared with an absorbed photon, an emitted fluorescence photon has:
questions.explanation: E = hc/λ. The emitted photon (520 nm) has a longer wavelength than the absorbed one (488 nm), so lower energy and lower frequency. The difference (Stokes shift) is lost as vibrational relaxation.

questions.stem: What is the approximate critical angle for light leaving the coverslip into air?
questions.explanation: sin θc = n2/n1 = 1.00/1.50 ≈ 0.67, so θc ≈ 42°. 30° would require sin θc = 0.5; 48° is its complement.

items.title: A Zinc–Copper Galvanic Cell
items.body: A galvanic cell is built from a zinc electrode in 1.0 M Zn(NO3)2 and a copper electrode in 1.0 M Cu(NO3)2, joined by a KNO3 salt bridge at 298 K. Standard reduction potentials: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu, E° = +0.34 V; Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Zn, E° = −0.76 V. The Faraday constant is approximately 96,500 C/mol e⁻.

questions.stem: What is the standard cell potential?
questions.explanation: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = 0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V. A galvanic cell has a positive E°cell; 0.42 V comes from adding the potentials directly.

questions.stem: At which electrode does oxidation occur?
questions.explanation: Zinc has the more negative reduction potential, so it is oxidized (Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻). Oxidation always occurs at the anode.

questions.stem: What is ΔG° for the cell reaction?
questions.explanation: ΔG° = −nFE° = −(2)(96,500)(1.10) ≈ −212,000 J/mol = −212 kJ/mol. −106 uses n = 1; −424 uses n = 4; a positive value would mean a nonspontaneous cell.

questions.stem: As the cell operates, how does its potential change?

choices.label: D
choices.text: It stays constant, because E° is fixed

questions.explanation: Q = [Zn²⁺]/[Cu²⁺]. As the cell runs, [Zn²⁺] rises and [Cu²⁺] falls, so Q increases and E = E° − (0.0592/n)log Q decreases toward zero.

questions.stem: Within the salt bridge, nitrate ions migrate:
questions.explanation: The anode compartment accumulates Zn²⁺ (positive charge), so anions such as NO3⁻ migrate toward it to maintain neutrality, while K⁺ migrates toward the cathode.

items.title: Blood Flow Through a Stenotic Artery
items.body: Laminar flow through a vessel follows Poiseuille's law, Q = πr⁴ΔP/(8ηL), where Q is volumetric flow rate, r is vessel radius, ΔP is the pressure difference, η is viscosity, and L is length. In atherosclerosis, plaque narrows the arterial lumen. Clinicians studied a segment of artery in which plaque reduced the radius to half its normal value, and modeled blood as an incompressible fluid.

questions.stem: If ΔP is unchanged, flow through the narrowed segment changes by what factor relative to normal?
questions.explanation: Q ∝ r⁴, so halving r gives (1/2)⁴ = 1/16 of normal flow. 1/4 would come from treating flow as proportional to cross-sectional area.

questions.stem: If the same volumetric flow rate passed through a region whose cross-sectional area is half that upstream, the fluid speed would:
questions.explanation: Continuity: A1v1 = A2v2. Halving area doubles speed for an incompressible fluid.

questions.stem: Compared with the wider upstream region, the static pressure inside the narrowed region is:

choices.label: B
choices.text: Higher, because the fluid speeds up

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lower, because the fluid speeds up

questions.explanation: Bernoulli: P + ½ρv² is constant along a streamline at equal height. Faster flow in the constriction means lower static pressure.

questions.stem: If a patient's blood viscosity doubled with all else constant, flow would:
questions.explanation: Q ∝ 1/η, so doubling viscosity halves flow.

items.title: Nucleophilic Substitution in Drug Synthesis
items.body: A chemist preparing a drug intermediate ran two substitution reactions. Reaction 1: (R)-2-bromobutane was treated with sodium cyanide in dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO). Reaction 2: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (tert-butyl bromide) was dissolved in a 1:1 water/ethanol mixture and warmed. Reaction 1 gave a single enantiomer of product, while Reaction 2 gave a mixture of an alcohol and an ether.

questions.stem: What is the product of Reaction 1?
questions.explanation: Secondary halide + strong nucleophile + polar aprotic solvent → SN2 with backside attack and inversion. CN keeps Br's priority rank (CN > ethyl > methyl > H), so inverting the geometry converts R to S. A racemic product would indicate SN1.

questions.stem: If the concentration of NaCN in Reaction 1 is doubled, the rate will:
questions.explanation: SN2 rate = k[substrate][nucleophile], first order in cyanide, so doubling [CN⁻] doubles the rate.

questions.stem: The rate-determining step of Reaction 2 is:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Simultaneous bond formation and bond breaking

choices.label: B
choices.text: Loss of bromide to form a carbocation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Attack of water on the substrate

questions.explanation: A tertiary halide in a polar protic solvent reacts by SN1. Unimolecular ionization to the tertiary carbocation is slow and rate-determining; nucleophilic capture and deprotonation are fast.

questions.stem: DMSO favors Reaction 1 primarily because it:

choices.label: C
choices.text: Solvates cations well but leaves anions poorly solvated and more reactive

questions.explanation: DMSO is polar aprotic. It solvates Na⁺ but cannot hydrogen-bond to CN⁻, leaving a 'naked', highly reactive nucleophile. SN2 has no carbocation intermediate.

questions.stem: Which is the best leaving group?
questions.explanation: Good leaving groups are weak bases. I⁻ is the conjugate base of the strongest acid (HI) and is large and polarizable, making it the best leaving group here.

items.title: Titration of Glycine
items.body: Glycine (H2N–CH2–COOH) was fully protonated in strong acid and then titrated with NaOH. The titration curve showed two buffering regions centered at pH 2.34 (pKa1, carboxyl group) and pH 9.60 (pKa2, ammonium group).

questions.stem: What is the isoelectric point of glycine?
questions.explanation: For an amino acid without an ionizable side chain, pI = (pKa1 + pKa2)/2 = (2.34 + 9.60)/2 = 5.97.

questions.stem: At physiological pH (7.4), the predominant form of glycine is:
questions.explanation: At 7.4 the pH is above pKa1 (carboxyl deprotonated) and below pKa2 (amine protonated), so the zwitterion dominates. The neutral uncharged form is never significant in water.

questions.stem: At pH 2.34, the average net charge on glycine is approximately:
questions.explanation: At pH = pKa1, half the molecules are +1 (fully protonated) and half are 0 (zwitterion), giving an average of +0.5.

questions.stem: How many equivalents of OH⁻ convert fully protonated glycine into its fully deprotonated form?
questions.explanation: Fully protonated glycine has two ionizable protons (COOH and NH3⁺), so two equivalents of base are required.

items.title: Thermodynamics of Protein Folding
items.body: Researchers used calorimetry to study folding of a small globular protein. For the reaction unfolded → folded, they measured ΔH = −200 kJ/mol and ΔS = −0.600 kJ/(mol·K), and assumed both were independent of temperature. They noted that the large favorable contribution from burying hydrophobic side chains is reflected in these values.

questions.stem: What is ΔG for folding at 300 K?
questions.explanation: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS = −200 − (300)(−0.600) = −200 + 180 = −20 kJ/mol, so folding is spontaneous at 300 K.

questions.stem: Above approximately what temperature does unfolding become spontaneous?
questions.explanation: ΔG = 0 when T = ΔH/ΔS = (−200)/(−0.600) ≈ 333 K. Above it, the −TΔS term dominates and ΔG for folding becomes positive.

questions.stem: The hydrophobic effect favors folding mainly by:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increasing the entropy of the surrounding water

choices.label: C
choices.text: Forming covalent bonds between nonpolar side chains

choices.label: D
choices.text: Decreasing the enthalpy of peptide bonds

questions.explanation: Exposed nonpolar groups force water into ordered cages. Burying them releases that water, increasing solvent entropy. The protein's own conformational entropy decreases on folding.

questions.stem: A chaperone protein that speeds folding would change which quantity?

choices.label: D
choices.text: The activation energy along the folding pathway

questions.explanation: Like a catalyst, a chaperone changes kinetics, not thermodynamics. ΔG, ΔH, and K are state functions or determined by them.

items.title: The Defibrillator Capacitor
items.body: An external defibrillator stores energy in a 100 µF capacitor charged to 2,000 V. When the paddles are applied, the capacitor discharges through the patient's chest, which can be modeled as a 50 Ω resistor. Engineers considered redesigning the capacitor with a dielectric material between its plates.

questions.stem: How much energy is stored in the charged capacitor?
How much charge is stored on the capacitor?
What is the time constant of the discharge?
If a dielectric with κ = 2 fills the gap and the capacitor is charged to the same 2,000 V, the stored energy becomes:
questions.explanation: C doubles with κ = 2. At fixed V, U = ½CV² doubles to 400 J.

items.title: Identifying an Unknown Solvent
items.body: A lab found an unlabeled bottle of a volatile liquid with molecular formula C3H6O. Its IR spectrum shows a strong, sharp absorption at 1715 cm⁻¹ and no broad absorption between 3200 and 3600 cm⁻¹. Its ¹H NMR spectrum shows a single singlet at 2.1 ppm integrating to 6H.

questions.stem: The unknown is most likely:
questions.explanation: The 1715 cm⁻¹ C=O stretch and one 6H singlet (two equivalent CH3 groups) identify acetone. Propanal would show an aldehyde H near 9.7 ppm; the alcohol would show a broad O–H stretch; oxetane has no C=O.

questions.stem: The absorption at 1715 cm⁻¹ corresponds to:
questions.explanation: Carbonyl stretches appear near 1700–1750 cm⁻¹. O–H is broad near 3300; sp³ C–H near 2900; C–O near 1000–1300.

questions.stem: If the sample were propanal, a signal near 9.7 ppm would appear because the aldehyde proton is:
questions.explanation: The electronegative oxygen and the magnetic anisotropy of the C=O bond deshield the aldehyde proton, shifting it far downfield.

questions.stem: How many degrees of unsaturation does C3H6O have?
questions.explanation: DoU = (2C + 2 − H)/2 = (6 + 2 − 6)/2 = 1. Oxygen does not affect the count. Here it is the C=O bond.

questions.stem: How many signals appear in the ¹³C NMR spectrum of the unknown?
questions.explanation: Acetone has two carbon environments: the two equivalent methyl carbons and the carbonyl carbon.

items.title: Hyperbaric Oxygen Therapy
items.body: In hyperbaric oxygen therapy, patients breathe 100% O2 inside a chamber pressurized to 3.0 atm. Dissolved O2 in plasma follows Henry's law, C = kH·P(O2). The therapy treats carbon monoxide poisoning and decompression sickness. At sea level, air is about 21% O2 at 1.0 atm.

questions.stem: What is the partial pressure of O2 the patient breathes in the chamber?
questions.explanation: Pure O2 at 3.0 atm total gives P(O2) = 1.00 × 3.0 = 3.0 atm. 0.63 atm would be air at 3.0 atm.

questions.stem: By roughly what factor does dissolved plasma O2 increase compared with breathing air at sea level?
questions.explanation: Henry's law: C ∝ P(O2). 3.0/0.21 ≈ 14. 3 compares total pressures only; 5 ignores the switch to pure O2 in the other direction.

questions.stem: A gas bubble in tissue at 3.0 atm is brought to 1.0 atm at constant temperature. Its volume:
questions.explanation: Boyle's law: P1V1 = P2V2, so dropping pressure from 3.0 to 1.0 atm triples the volume, which is why rapid decompression is dangerous.

questions.stem: High P(O2) speeds removal of CO from hemoglobin primarily because:

choices.label: A
choices.text: O2 oxidizes CO to CO2 in the blood

choices.label: D
choices.text: O2 competes with CO for the same heme binding sites

questions.explanation: CO and O2 bind the same heme iron. Raising P(O2) shifts the binding equilibrium toward oxyhemoglobin (Le Châtelier), displacing CO.

items.stem: What is the ground-state electron configuration of Fe³⁺?
items.explanation: Fe is [Ar]3d⁶4s². Transition metals lose 4s electrons first, then 3d: removing two 4s and one 3d electron gives [Ar]3d⁵.

items.stem: A radioactive isotope has a half-life of 5 days. How much of an 80 g sample remains after 15 days?
items.explanation: 15 days = 3 half-lives: 80 → 40 → 20 → 10 g.

items.stem: If sound intensity increases by a factor of 100, the sound level increases by:
items.explanation: β = 10 log(I/I0), so a 100× increase adds 10 log(100) = 20 dB.

items.stem: Which amino acid is achiral?
items.explanation: Glycine's side chain is H, so its α-carbon has two identical substituents and is not a stereocenter.

items.stem: An ideal gas in a rigid container is heated from 300 K to 600 K. Its pressure:
items.explanation: At constant V and n, P ∝ T (Gay-Lussac). Doubling absolute temperature doubles pressure.

items.stem: As an ambulance approaches a stationary listener, the siren frequency the listener hears is:
items.explanation: Doppler effect: a source moving toward the observer compresses wavefronts, raising the observed frequency.

items.stem: For N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), ΔH < 0, raising the temperature will:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Shift equilibrium left and decrease K

choices.label: C
choices.text: Shift equilibrium left with K unchanged

choices.label: D
choices.text: Shift equilibrium right and increase K

items.explanation: For an exothermic reaction, heat acts as a product. Adding heat shifts left, and K decreases because K is temperature-dependent.

items.stem: What is the oxidation state of Mn in KMnO4?
items.explanation: K is +1 and each O is −2 (total −8), so Mn = +7 for a neutral compound.

items.stem: A 10 N force pulls a box 5.0 m across the floor at 60° above the horizontal. How much work does the force do?
items.explanation: W = Fd cos θ = (10)(5.0)(cos 60°) = 25 J. 43 J uses sin 60°; 50 J ignores the angle.

items.stem: Which compound is the strongest acid?
items.explanation: Three electron-withdrawing fluorines stabilize the carboxylate of trifluoroacetic acid (pKa ≈ 0.2), making it far stronger than acetic acid (4.76), phenol (10), or ethanol (16).

items.stem: Acetic acid heated with ethanol and catalytic H2SO4 produces:
items.explanation: Fischer esterification: carboxylic acid + alcohol under acid catalysis gives an ester plus water.

items.stem: A 0.0020 m³ object is fully submerged in water (ρ = 1,000 kg/m³, g = 10 m/s²). What is the buoyant force?
items.explanation: Archimedes: F = ρVg = (1,000)(0.0020)(10) = 20 N, independent of the object's own density.

items.stem: Two 6 Ω resistors in parallel are connected to a 12 V battery. What current does the battery supply?
items.explanation: R_eq = (6 × 6)/(6 + 6) = 3 Ω, so I = V/R = 12/3 = 4 A. 1 A uses the series value of 12 Ω.

items.stem: Which bond links adjacent nucleotides in the DNA backbone?
items.explanation: Phosphodiester bonds join the 3′ carbon of one sugar to the 5′ carbon of the next. Glycosidic bonds attach bases to sugars; hydrogen bonds pair bases across strands.

items.stem: 5.85 g of NaCl (58.5 g/mol) is dissolved in water to make 500 mL of solution. What is the molarity?
items.explanation: 5.85/58.5 = 0.100 mol, and 0.100 mol / 0.500 L = 0.200 M. 0.1 M forgets to divide by volume.

exams.title: FL1: Bio/Biochem
exams.description: Full-length Bio/Biochem section: 10 passages and 59 questions in 95 minutes.

items.title: Knocking Out TLR4 in Macrophages
items.body: Researchers used CRISPR-Cas9 with a guide RNA targeting exon 2 of Tlr4 to generate knockout (KO) mouse macrophages. Western blotting of cell lysates was probed for TLR4 (~95 kDa) and β-actin (~42 kDa). Wild-type (WT) and KO cells were then stimulated with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) from gram-negative bacteria, and TNF-α secretion was measured by ELISA.
items.figure: Figure 1: Western blot — WT lane shows bands at 95 and 42 kDa; KO lane shows only the 42 kDa band. ELISA: WT + LPS ≈ 1,200 pg/mL TNF-α; KO + LPS ≈ 80 pg/mL; unstimulated cells of both types < 50 pg/mL.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of probing for β-actin?

choices.label: C
choices.text: To show equal protein was loaded in each lane

questions.explanation: β-actin is a constitutively expressed loading control. Equal β-actin bands show that the missing TLR4 band in KO cells reflects absent protein, not less sample loaded.

questions.stem: The guide RNA's role is to:

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cut the DNA at the target site

choices.label: D
choices.text: Direct Cas9 to the target sequence by complementary base pairing

questions.explanation: The sgRNA base-pairs with the target DNA and recruits Cas9, which makes the cut. Repair is done by host machinery; mRNA silencing describes RNAi.

questions.stem: Loss of TLR4 protein most likely resulted from:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Error-prone non-homologous end joining creating a frameshift

choices.label: B
choices.text: Degradation of TLR4 by the proteasome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Homology-directed repair inserting a functional copy

questions.explanation: Without a repair template, the Cas9 break is repaired by NHEJ, which often introduces small insertions or deletions. A frameshift creates a premature stop codon, so no full-length protein is made.

questions.stem: TLR4 detecting LPS is an example of:
questions.explanation: Toll-like receptors are germline-encoded pattern-recognition receptors that detect conserved microbial molecules such as LPS, a hallmark of innate immunity.

items.title: Insulin Signaling and GLUT4
items.body: Insulin binds its cell-surface receptor, triggering receptor autophosphorylation on tyrosine residues and activation of the PI3K–Akt pathway. In skeletal muscle and adipose tissue, Akt signaling causes vesicles containing the glucose transporter GLUT4 to fuse with the plasma membrane. In type 2 diabetes, tissues show reduced responsiveness to insulin (insulin resistance).

questions.stem: The insulin receptor is best classified as a:
questions.explanation: Autophosphorylation on tyrosines after ligand binding defines a receptor tyrosine kinase. Nuclear receptors bind lipophilic ligands such as steroids.

questions.stem: Glucose moves through GLUT4 by:
questions.explanation: GLUT transporters move glucose down its concentration gradient using a carrier protein, without ATP. That is facilitated diffusion. SGLT transporters use secondary active transport.

questions.stem: Which tissue takes up glucose largely independently of insulin?
questions.explanation: Neurons rely on insulin-independent GLUT1 and GLUT3, keeping the brain's glucose supply steady. Muscle and fat depend on insulin-stimulated GLUT4.

questions.stem: In the liver, insulin promotes:
questions.explanation: Insulin is the fed-state hormone: it stimulates glycogen synthesis and inhibits glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, and ketogenesis.

questions.stem: Insulin is secreted by:

choices.label: A
choices.text: δ cells of the pancreatic islets

choices.label: B
choices.text: β cells of the pancreatic islets

choices.label: C
choices.text: Acinar cells of the exocrine pancreas

choices.label: D
choices.text: α cells of the pancreatic islets

questions.explanation: β cells secrete insulin; α cells secrete glucagon; δ cells secrete somatostatin; acinar cells secrete digestive enzymes.

items.title: An Uncoupler of Oxidative Phosphorylation
items.body: 2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP) is a lipophilic weak acid that picks up protons in the mitochondrial intermembrane space, diffuses across the inner membrane, and releases them in the matrix. It was once sold as a weight-loss drug before being banned due to fatal hyperthermia. Isolated mitochondria were given succinate as substrate, and O2 consumption and ATP production were measured before and after adding DNP.

questions.stem: After DNP is added, O2 consumption will:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Stop, because complex IV is inhibited

choices.label: C
choices.text: Decrease, because the gradient is lost

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increase, because the electron transport chain is no longer slowed by the gradient

questions.explanation: A steep proton gradient normally slows the ETC (respiratory control). Dissipating it removes that brake, so electron flow and O2 consumption increase.

questions.stem: ATP production by ATP synthase will:

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reverse direction only in the matrix

questions.explanation: ATP synthase is driven by protons flowing back through it. DNP provides a bypass, so less proton-motive force drives ATP synthesis.

questions.stem: The energy from electron transport in DNP-treated mitochondria is mainly released as:
questions.explanation: With the gradient dissipated, energy from substrate oxidation is lost as heat, explaining the hyperthermia. Brown fat's UCP1 does the same thing physiologically.

questions.stem: Which complex transfers electrons directly to O2?
questions.explanation: Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase) reduces O2 to H2O. Complex II accepts electrons from succinate.

questions.stem: In functioning mitochondria, the proton concentration is highest in the:
questions.explanation: Complexes I, III, and IV pump protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space, so it has the higher [H⁺] (lower pH).

items.title: Loop Diuretics
items.body: Furosemide is a loop diuretic that inhibits the Na⁺–K⁺–2Cl⁻ cotransporter (NKCC2) on the apical membrane of the nephron. It is used to treat fluid overload in heart failure. A common side effect is low serum potassium.

questions.stem: Furosemide acts mainly in the:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle

questions.explanation: NKCC2 is located on the apical membrane of the thick ascending limb, the segment loop diuretics are named for.

questions.stem: Furosemide will cause urine volume to:
questions.explanation: Blocking NaCl reabsorption leaves more solute in the tubule and weakens the medullary gradient, so less water is reabsorbed and urine volume rises.

questions.stem: Low serum potassium results mainly because:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Furosemide blocks K⁺ absorption in the gut

choices.label: B
choices.text: More Na⁺ reaches the collecting duct, increasing K⁺ secretion

questions.explanation: Increased distal Na⁺ delivery drives Na⁺ reabsorption via ENaC in principal cells, making the lumen more negative and promoting K⁺ secretion. Volume loss also raises aldosterone.

questions.stem: Which hormone increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct?
questions.explanation: ADH (vasopressin) inserts aquaporin-2 channels into collecting duct cells. ANP promotes natriuresis; renin is an enzyme.

items.title: Hemophilia A in a Family
items.body: Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by mutations in the gene for clotting factor VIII. A woman whose father had hemophilia A has a normal clotting profile. She and her husband, who does not have hemophilia, are planning a family.

questions.stem: What is the probability that their son will have hemophilia A?
questions.explanation: Her father passed her his affected X, so she is a carrier (XᴴXʰ). Each son receives one of her X chromosomes, so the chance is 1/2.

questions.stem: What is the probability that their daughter will have hemophilia A?
questions.explanation: Daughters receive the father's normal X, so at worst they are carriers.

questions.stem: If an affected man has children with a woman who is not a carrier, his daughters will be:
questions.explanation: Every daughter gets his X carrying the mutation plus a normal X from her mother, so all daughters are carriers. Sons get his Y and are unaffected.

questions.stem: Factor VIII deficiency most directly impairs:

choices.label: A
choices.text: The coagulation cascade leading to fibrin formation

questions.explanation: Factor VIII is part of the intrinsic coagulation pathway (secondary hemostasis). Platelet plug formation (primary hemostasis) is largely normal.

questions.stem: X-linked recessive disorders are more common in males because males are:

choices.label: A
choices.text: More likely to have new mutations

questions.explanation: Males have one X, so a single recessive allele is expressed. Females need two copies.

items.title: Metabolism and Antigen Presentation
items.body: Tumors consume large amounts of methionine, depleting it from the surrounding environment. Methionine is required for protein synthesis and is converted to S-adenosylmethionine (SAM). Researchers hypothesized that methionine restriction impairs the ability of macrophages to process and present tumor antigens to CD8⁺ T cells through MHC class I.

questions.stem: MHC class I molecules present peptides to:
questions.explanation: MHC I presents to CD8⁺ T cells; MHC II presents to CD4⁺ T cells.

questions.stem: Which cells express MHC class I?
questions.explanation: MHC I is on essentially all nucleated cells, letting CD8⁺ T cells survey any infected or cancerous cell. Mature red blood cells lack nuclei and MHC I.

questions.stem: Peptides loaded onto MHC I are typically generated by:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lysosomal proteases, then loaded in endosomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: The proteasome, then transported into the ER by TAP

questions.explanation: Cytosolic proteins are degraded by the proteasome, and peptides enter the ER via TAP for loading onto MHC I. The lysosomal route feeds MHC II.

questions.stem: SAM derived from methionine functions mainly as a:
questions.explanation: SAM is the main cellular methyl donor, used for DNA and histone methylation among other reactions. ATP donates phosphate; NADH carries electrons; CoA carries acyl groups.

items.title: Tetrodotoxin and the Action Potential
items.body: Tetrodotoxin (TTX), found in pufferfish, binds voltage-gated sodium channels and blocks the pore. Researchers recorded from a squid giant axon before and after TTX application while stimulating it with a depolarizing current.

questions.stem: After TTX application, stimulation will:

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fail to produce the rising phase of an action potential

questions.explanation: The upstroke depends on Na⁺ influx through voltage-gated Na⁺ channels. Blocking them prevents the action potential.

questions.stem: The resting membrane potential is established mainly by:
questions.explanation: At rest the membrane is most permeable to K⁺ via leak channels, so the resting potential (~−70 mV) sits near K⁺'s equilibrium potential. The Na⁺/K⁺ pump maintains the gradients.

questions.stem: Repolarization is caused mainly by:
questions.explanation: After Na⁺ channels inactivate, voltage-gated K⁺ channels open and K⁺ efflux returns the membrane toward rest.

questions.stem: Myelin increases conduction velocity by:

choices.label: C
choices.text: Allowing saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increasing the number of Na⁺ channels along the whole axon

questions.explanation: Myelin insulates the axon and decreases capacitance, so the signal jumps between nodes of Ranvier, where Na⁺ channels cluster.

items.title: Regulation of the lac Operon
items.body: E. coli expresses the lac operon genes (lacZ, lacY, lacA) to use lactose as a carbon source. Transcription is controlled by the LacI repressor binding the operator and by the catabolite activator protein (CAP), which binds DNA when complexed with cAMP. Researchers grew wild-type and mutant strains in different media and measured β-galactosidase activity.

questions.stem: β-galactosidase expression will be highest when:
questions.explanation: High expression needs the repressor removed (lactose present) and CAP–cAMP bound, which requires high cAMP when glucose is absent.

questions.stem: A lacI mutation producing a repressor that cannot bind the operator will cause:

choices.label: C
choices.text: Expression only with high cAMP and glucose

questions.explanation: Without a functional repressor binding the operator, the operon is transcribed regardless of lactose (constitutive), though still modulated by CAP.

questions.stem: cAMP levels in E. coli are high when:
questions.explanation: Glucose transport inhibits adenylate cyclase. When glucose is scarce, cAMP rises and forms CAP–cAMP, which boosts transcription.

questions.stem: Lactose induces the operon because allolactose:

choices.label: C
choices.text: Binds the repressor and lowers its affinity for the operator

questions.explanation: Allolactose is an allosteric inducer: it binds LacI and changes its shape so it releases the operator.

items.title: Allele Frequencies in an Island Population
items.body: An island population of 1,000 lizards was surveyed for an autosomal recessive trait causing pale coloration. 160 lizards showed the pale phenotype. Researchers assumed the population was in Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium for this gene.

questions.stem: What is the frequency of the recessive allele?
questions.explanation: q² = 160/1,000 = 0.16, so q = 0.40. 0.16 is the genotype frequency; 0.60 is p.

questions.stem: What fraction of the population is heterozygous?
questions.explanation: 2pq = 2(0.60)(0.40) = 0.48. 0.24 omits the factor of 2.

questions.stem: What fraction is homozygous dominant?
A storm kills a random 90% of the lizards. Allele frequencies in survivors may change mainly due to:
questions.explanation: A random reduction in population size is a bottleneck. Chance changes in allele frequency, unrelated to fitness, are genetic drift.

questions.stem: Lizards from the mainland begin arriving on rafts and breeding. This violates the Hardy–Weinberg assumption of:
questions.explanation: Migration introduces alleles from another population (gene flow), changing allele frequencies.

items.title: Carnitine Deficiency
items.body: Long-chain fatty acids are activated to acyl-CoA in the cytosol and must be transported into the mitochondrial matrix for β-oxidation. Patients with primary carnitine deficiency develop muscle weakness and, during fasting, low blood glucose with abnormally low ketone levels.

questions.stem: Carnitine's role is to:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Carry acetyl groups out of the mitochondria for fatty acid synthesis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Shuttle long-chain acyl groups across the inner mitochondrial membrane

questions.explanation: The carnitine shuttle (CPT-I, translocase, CPT-II) moves long-chain acyl groups into the matrix. Citrate carries acetyl groups out for fatty acid synthesis.

questions.stem: Why do these patients become hypoglycemic with low ketones during fasting?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased glucose uptake by the brain

choices.label: D
choices.text: Impaired β-oxidation limits ketone production and the energy that supports gluconeogenesis

questions.explanation: Without β-oxidation, the liver cannot make acetyl-CoA for ketogenesis or the ATP and NADH that power gluconeogenesis, producing hypoketotic hypoglycemia.

questions.stem: Each round of β-oxidation produces:
questions.explanation: Each cycle has an FAD-dependent dehydrogenation, a hydration, an NAD⁺-dependent oxidation, and a thiolysis that releases one acetyl-CoA.

questions.stem: Complete β-oxidation of palmitoyl-CoA (16 carbons) yields how many acetyl-CoA?
questions.explanation: 16 carbons / 2 = 8 acetyl-CoA, produced over 7 rounds (the final round releases two).

items.stem: Which enzyme relieves supercoiling ahead of the replication fork?
items.explanation: Topoisomerases cut and reseal DNA to relieve torsional strain created by unwinding. Helicase unwinds; primase makes RNA primers; ligase seals nicks.

items.stem: Which organelle is the main site of lipid synthesis?
items.explanation: Smooth ER synthesizes lipids and steroids and detoxifies drugs. Rough ER synthesizes secreted and membrane proteins.

items.stem: How many of the 64 codons specify amino acids?
items.explanation: Three codons (UAA, UAG, UGA) are stop codons, leaving 61 sense codons.

items.stem: Antibodies are secreted by:
items.explanation: Plasma cells are differentiated B cells that secrete antibodies.

items.stem: Pulmonary surfactant is produced by:
items.explanation: Type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant, which lowers surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse. Type I cells form the gas-exchange surface.

items.stem: Crossing over occurs during:
items.explanation: Homologous chromosomes pair as tetrads and exchange segments at chiasmata during prophase I.

items.stem: Which hormone is released from the posterior pituitary?
items.explanation: The posterior pituitary releases oxytocin and ADH, which are made in the hypothalamus. The others come from the anterior pituitary.

items.stem: A rise in blood CO2 and a fall in pH shift the hemoglobin–O2 dissociation curve:
items.explanation: The Bohr effect: H⁺ and CO2 stabilize the low-affinity T state, shifting the curve right and promoting O2 unloading in active tissues.

items.stem: Branch points in glycogen are formed by:
items.explanation: Glycogen chains are α-1,4 linked, with α-1,6 branches added by branching enzyme. β-1,4 bonds are found in cellulose.

items.stem: Okazaki fragments are synthesized on the:
items.explanation: DNA polymerase works only 5′→3′, so the lagging strand is made discontinuously in short Okazaki fragments.

items.stem: Bile is produced by the:
items.explanation: Hepatocytes produce bile; the gallbladder stores and concentrates it.

items.stem: A point mutation that changes a codon to UAG is a:
items.explanation: UAG is a stop codon, so the mutation truncates the protein: a nonsense mutation.

items.stem: Loss-of-function mutations in p53 promote cancer because p53 normally:

choices.label: B
choices.text: Halts the cell cycle or triggers apoptosis after DNA damage

items.explanation: p53 is a tumor suppressor that arrests the cycle at G1/S for repair or triggers apoptosis. Losing it lets damaged cells keep dividing.

items.stem: One primary spermatocyte produces how many mature sperm?
items.explanation: Meiosis I and II yield four haploid spermatids, which mature into four sperm. Oogenesis yields one egg plus polar bodies.

items.stem: Pepsin is secreted as pepsinogen by:
items.explanation: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen, which HCl from parietal cells converts to active pepsin. G cells secrete gastrin.

exams.title: FL1: Psych/Soc
exams.description: Full-length Psych/Soc section: 10 passages and 59 questions in 95 minutes.

items.title: Remembering a Word List
items.body: Participants heard lists of 15 unrelated words at one word per 2 seconds and then wrote down as many as they could recall in any order. In Condition A, recall began immediately. In Condition B, participants counted backward by threes for 30 seconds before recall. In Condition A, recall was highest for the first few and last few words. In Condition B, recall stayed high for the first few words but fell for the last few.

questions.stem: Better recall of the first words in both conditions is called the:
questions.explanation: Early items get more rehearsal and are transferred into long-term memory: the primacy effect.

questions.stem: The counting task in Condition B eliminated the:

choices.label: B
choices.text: Recency effect, by displacing items from short-term memory

choices.label: D
choices.text: Primacy effect, by blocking long-term storage

questions.explanation: Recent items are held in short-term memory, and a 30-second distractor displaces them. Primacy items in long-term memory are unaffected.

questions.stem: The typical capacity of short-term memory is about:
questions.explanation: Miller's classic estimate is 7 ± 2 items, which can be extended with chunking.

questions.stem: Participants told to think about each word's meaning recalled more words. This supports:
questions.explanation: Deeper (semantic) processing produces more durable encoding than shallow processing: the levels-of-processing framework.

questions.stem: A patient with bilateral hippocampal damage would most likely show:

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inability to form new explicit long-term memories

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of procedural skills like bike riding

questions.explanation: Hippocampal damage causes anterograde amnesia for declarative memory (as in patient H.M.). Older memories, procedural memory, and digit span are relatively spared.

items.title: Who Helps in an Emergency?
items.body: In a study, participants completed a survey alone, with two confederates, or with five confederates. Smoke began pouring through a vent. Confederates were instructed to ignore the smoke. The percentage of participants who reported the smoke within 4 minutes was 75% alone, 38% with two confederates, and 10% with five confederates.

questions.stem: The decline in reporting as group size grew best illustrates:
questions.explanation: People are less likely to help when others are present: the bystander effect.

questions.stem: Participants who saw calm confederates concluded there was no emergency. This reflects:
questions.explanation: When each person privately doubts but sees others looking unconcerned, everyone wrongly concludes nothing is wrong: pluralistic ignorance, a form of informational social influence.

questions.stem: In this study, the number of confederates is the:
questions.explanation: Researchers manipulated group size, so it is the independent variable. Reporting rate is the dependent variable.

questions.stem: Which action by someone needing help would most reduce the bystander effect?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Shouting for help to the crowd generally

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pointing to one person and asking them directly

questions.explanation: Singling out one person removes diffusion of responsibility, because that person now clearly owns the responsibility to act.

items.title: Sleep in Medical Residents
items.body: Researchers recorded EEGs in medical residents sleeping after a normal workday and after a 28-hour shift. After the extended shift, residents entered REM sleep sooner and spent a greater proportion of the night in REM. Separately, residents working night shifts showed disrupted secretion of a hormone that normally rises in darkness.

questions.stem: EEG delta waves dominate during:
questions.explanation: Stage N3 (slow-wave sleep) is characterized by high-amplitude, low-frequency delta waves. N2 shows sleep spindles and K-complexes.

questions.stem: Which feature characterizes REM sleep?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Beta-like EEG activity with skeletal muscle atonia

questions.explanation: REM shows an EEG resembling wakefulness, vivid dreaming, rapid eye movements, and paralysis of most skeletal muscles. Sleepwalking occurs in N3.

questions.stem: The increased REM after the 28-hour shift is called:
questions.explanation: After REM deprivation, the body compensates by entering REM sooner and spending more time in it: REM rebound.

questions.stem: The hormone that rises in darkness is secreted by the:
questions.explanation: The pineal gland secretes melatonin in darkness under control of the suprachiasmatic nucleus.

items.title: First-Generation College Students
items.body: A sociologist interviewed first-generation college students, whose parents did not attend college. Many reported not knowing how to use office hours, network with professors, or apply for research positions, while classmates from college-educated families learned these norms at home. Despite this, many students said success depends only on hard work and talent.

questions.stem: A first-generation student who becomes a physician is experiencing:
questions.explanation: Moving to a higher social position than one's parents is intergenerational upward mobility.

questions.stem: Familiarity with norms such as using office hours is an example of:
questions.explanation: Bourdieu's cultural capital is non-financial knowledge, skills, and dispositions that confer advantage. Social capital refers to networks of relationships.

questions.stem: The students' belief that success depends only on effort and talent reflects:
questions.explanation: A meritocracy is a system in which advancement is based on individual merit. The passage suggests unequal cultural capital complicates that belief.

questions.stem: When children of college-educated parents are advantaged in reaching the same status, inequality persists through:
questions.explanation: Social reproduction is the transmission of social inequality across generations through structures such as cultural capital and education.

questions.stem: In Max Weber's view of stratification, 'status' refers to:
questions.explanation: Weber separated class (economic position), status (prestige), and party (power).

items.title: Engineered to Keep You Playing
items.body: A mobile game awards rare items unpredictably after some number of loot-box openings, sometimes after 2 openings, sometimes after 30. A separate in-game reward arrives exactly every 24 hours. Researchers noticed that when the rare-item feature was removed, many players opened loot boxes even more frequently for a short time before stopping.

questions.stem: The loot-box rewards follow which reinforcement schedule?
questions.explanation: Rewards depend on a varying number of responses: variable-ratio, the schedule most resistant to extinction (like slot machines).

questions.stem: The daily reward produces which response pattern?

choices.label: D
choices.text: A scalloped pattern with more responding near the reward time

questions.explanation: Fixed-interval schedules produce a scallop: responding drops after reinforcement and increases as the next reward time nears.

questions.stem: The temporary increase in opening after the feature was removed is a(n):
questions.explanation: When reinforcement stops, behavior often briefly intensifies before declining: an extinction burst.

questions.stem: A player's parents stop nagging once homework is done, and homework completion increases. This is:
questions.explanation: Removing an aversive stimulus (nagging) to increase a behavior is negative reinforcement.

items.title: Children's Thinking
items.body: A developmental psychologist tested children of different ages. A 7-month-old stopped searching when a toy was hidden under a blanket. A 4-year-old said a tall, thin glass held more juice than a short, wide glass with the same amount. The 4-year-old also assumed the researcher could see the same picture she saw, even though it faced away from him.

questions.stem: By the end of which Piagetian stage does the infant develop object permanence?
questions.explanation: Object permanence develops during the sensorimotor stage (birth to ~2 years).

questions.stem: The 4-year-old's juice error shows a lack of:
questions.explanation: Conservation, understanding that quantity is unchanged by shape, emerges in the concrete operational stage (~7–11 years).

questions.stem: Assuming the researcher sees what she sees is:
questions.explanation: Preoperational children struggle to take others' perspectives: egocentrism.

questions.stem: A child who calls all four-legged animals 'dog,' then learns cats are different and creates a new category, is showing:
questions.explanation: Modifying or creating a schema to fit new information is accommodation. Fitting new information into an existing schema is assimilation.

items.title: Stress Before an Exam
items.body: Students preparing for a high-stakes exam reported high stress. Salivary cortisol was elevated in the weeks before the exam, and students reported more colds. One student made a detailed study schedule and met with a tutor; another spent evenings watching TV to avoid thinking about the exam.

questions.stem: The correct sequence of the HPA axis response is:
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus releases CRH, the anterior pituitary releases ACTH, and the adrenal cortex releases cortisol.

questions.stem: The increase in colds is best explained by cortisol's effect of:
questions.explanation: Chronically elevated cortisol is immunosuppressive. It also raises blood glucose.

questions.stem: Prolonged stress leading to depleted resources corresponds to which stage of Selye's general adaptation syndrome?
questions.explanation: The GAS stages are alarm, resistance, and exhaustion. Exhaustion follows prolonged stress and increases illness vulnerability.

questions.stem: The student who made a study schedule and met with a tutor is using:
questions.explanation: Directly tackling the source of stress is problem-focused coping. Watching TV to avoid thinking is avoidance.

items.title: Smartphones and Attention
items.body: Researchers randomly assigned 120 college students to leave their silenced phone on the desk, in their bag, or in another room. Participants then completed a working-memory task. Scores were highest in the other-room condition, and the difference was statistically significant (p = 0.02). A research assistant who knew each participant's condition scored the open-ended portion of the task.

questions.stem: The independent variable is:
questions.explanation: Phone location is manipulated; working-memory score is the measured dependent variable.

questions.stem: Random assignment allows the researchers to:

choices.label: B
choices.text: Infer that phone location caused the score differences

choices.label: D
choices.text: Eliminate the need for a control group

questions.explanation: Random assignment distributes participant differences evenly across groups, supporting causal inference (internal validity). Generalization depends on sampling.

questions.stem: The scoring procedure most threatens validity through:
questions.explanation: A scorer who knows the conditions may unconsciously score in line with the hypothesis. Blinding the scorer would fix this.

questions.stem: Using only college students primarily limits:
questions.explanation: A narrow sample limits generalizability to other populations, which is external validity.

questions.stem: p = 0.02 means:

choices.label: B
choices.text: There is a 2% chance the hypothesis is false

choices.label: D
choices.text: If the null hypothesis were true, results this extreme would occur about 2% of the time

questions.explanation: A p-value is the probability of data at least this extreme assuming the null is true. It is not the probability that the hypothesis is false and says nothing about effect size.

items.title: Labels and Identity
items.body: A teenager was arrested once for shoplifting. Afterward, teachers treated him as a 'troublemaker,' and he began skipping school and spending time with others who had been in trouble. He described feeling that people now saw him only as a criminal. At work, he acted polished in front of customers but relaxed with coworkers in the break room.

questions.stem: The idea that being labeled deviant led to further deviance reflects:
questions.explanation: Labeling theory holds that a deviant label can push someone toward a deviant identity and further (secondary) deviance.

questions.stem: Being seen only as a criminal suggests 'criminal' has become his:
questions.explanation: A master status overshadows a person's other statuses and dominates how others see them.

questions.stem: His polished behavior with customers versus the break room illustrates:

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dramaturgical analysis (front stage vs back stage)

questions.explanation: Goffman's dramaturgy compares social life to a performance: front stage for an audience, back stage where people relax.

questions.stem: Teachers' expectations that he would cause trouble, leading to his misbehavior, is a:
questions.explanation: An expectation that elicits behavior confirming it is a self-fulfilling prophecy.

questions.stem: Goffman described a stigmatized trait as producing a:
questions.explanation: Goffman called stigma an attribute that discredits a person, reducing them to a 'spoiled identity.'

items.title: Neighborhood and Health
items.body: A public health team compared two neighborhoods in the same city. Neighborhood A had high incomes, grocery stores, and parks. Neighborhood B had lower incomes, convenience stores but no full-service grocery store, and higher air pollution. Life expectancy differed by 12 years. Health also improved step by step across income levels, not just between the richest and poorest.

questions.stem: Income, food access, and pollution are examples of:
questions.explanation: Social determinants of health are the conditions in which people are born, live, and work that shape health.

questions.stem: An area lacking full-service grocery stores is often called a:
questions.explanation: A food desert is an area with limited access to affordable, nutritious food.

questions.stem: Health improving at each step up the income ladder is called the:
questions.explanation: The social gradient describes a stepwise relationship between socioeconomic position and health across the whole spectrum.

questions.stem: If zoning policies placed polluting factories mainly in Neighborhood B, this would exemplify:
questions.explanation: Discrimination embedded in policies and institutions, rather than individual attitudes, is institutional discrimination (here, environmental injustice).

items.stem: According to Maslow, which needs must be met first?
items.explanation: Maslow's hierarchy starts with physiological needs, followed by safety, belonging, esteem, and self-actualization.

items.stem: A smoker who knows smoking is harmful says 'my grandpa smoked and lived to 95.' This reduces:
items.explanation: Holding conflicting beliefs and behaviors creates discomfort (dissonance), which people reduce by changing beliefs or justifying behavior.

items.stem: The minimum stimulus intensity detected 50% of the time is the:
items.explanation: The absolute threshold is the lowest intensity detected half the time. The difference threshold (JND) is the smallest detectable change.

items.stem: Damage to Broca's area most likely causes:

choices.label: B
choices.text: Effortful, halting speech with relatively intact comprehension

items.explanation: Broca's (expressive) aphasia impairs speech production. Wernicke's aphasia produces fluent but nonsensical speech.

items.stem: According to Erikson, the central crisis of adolescence is:
items.explanation: Erikson's adolescent stage is identity vs role confusion. Intimacy vs isolation follows in young adulthood.

items.stem: A cohesive team ignores warnings and makes a poor decision to preserve harmony. This is:
items.explanation: Groupthink is prioritizing consensus over critical evaluation, which leads to poor decisions.

items.stem: Durkheim used 'anomie' to describe:

choices.label: D
choices.text: A lack of clear social norms

items.explanation: Anomie is a breakdown of social norms that leaves individuals without guidance, which Durkheim linked to suicide rates.

items.stem: A skilled pianist plays better in front of an audience. This is:
items.explanation: The presence of others improves performance on well-learned or simple tasks and impairs it on complex or new tasks.

items.stem: Searching only for evidence that supports one's existing belief is:
items.explanation: Confirmation bias is seeking or favoring information that confirms prior beliefs.

items.stem: The mesolimbic dopamine pathway is most associated with:
items.explanation: The mesolimbic pathway (ventral tegmental area to nucleus accumbens) mediates reward and is implicated in addiction. The nigrostriatal pathway controls movement.

items.stem: Which is a positive symptom of schizophrenia?
items.explanation: Positive symptoms add abnormal experiences, such as hallucinations and delusions. Negative symptoms are deficits, such as flat affect and avolition.

items.stem: Symbolic interactionism focuses on:

choices.label: B
choices.text: How individuals create meaning through everyday interaction

items.explanation: Symbolic interactionism is a micro-level theory about meaning made through interaction and symbols. Conflict theory and functionalism are macro-level.

items.stem: In the demographic transition model, stage 2 is marked by:

choices.label: B
choices.text: Falling birth rates with low death rates

choices.label: C
choices.text: Falling death rates with high birth rates

items.explanation: Stage 2 sees death rates drop from better sanitation and medicine while birth rates stay high, producing rapid population growth.

items.stem: In signal detection theory, saying a tone was present when it was not is a:
items.explanation: A false alarm is a 'yes' response with no signal. A hit is a 'yes' with a signal; a miss is a 'no' with a signal.

items.stem: The James–Lange theory holds that:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Physiological arousal comes first and is interpreted as emotion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Emotion and arousal occur at the same time

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cognitive labeling of arousal produces emotion

items.explanation: James–Lange: we feel afraid because we notice our body trembling. Cannon–Bard says they occur simultaneously; Schachter–Singer adds cognitive labeling.
